research.abstract: Introduction The development of accurate and reliable diagnostic tools for tuberculosis remains a global health challenge. However, currently antibody-based assays lack sufficient sensitivity (30-40%). This study aimed to construct a multi-epitope fusion protein (Mtb6-Avi) and evaluate it for serological diagnosis and the assessment of radiographic severity. Methods The diagnostic antigen was designed based on 11 B-cell epitopes derived from six highly expressed Mycobacterium tuberculosis proteins. In this retrospective, single-center study, serum samples from 251 patients with pulmonary tuberculosis, 98 patients with non-TB pneumonia, and 20 healthy controls were analyzed by ELISA. A SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) analysis was used to explore the factors associated with radiographic severity. Results Serum Mtb6-Avi-binding antibody levels were significantly higher in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis than in patients with non-TB pneumonia and healthy controls (P < 0.001). The ROC curve yielded an AUC of 0.856 (95% CI, 0.819-0.893) with a sensitivity of 74.1% (95% CI, 68.2-79.4) and a specificity of 83.9% (95% CI, 76.0-90.0), indicating moderate diagnostic accuracy in this cohort. In a head-to-head comparison among 170 PTB patients without tumour or immune disorders, in whom both assays were performed, the sensitivity of the Mtb6-Avi assay was higher than that of one commercial TB antibody detection kit (74.1% vs 35.3%; McNemar's exact test, P < 0.001). In an exploratory SHAP analysis, C-reactive protein and the Mtb6-Avi-binding antibody had the highest mean absolute SHAP values among the predictors examined; these rankings describe associations within the model and require confirmation in independent cohorts. Conclusion In this retrospective cohort, the multi-epitope antigen was associated with higher sensitivity than one commercial serodiagnostic kit in the 170 patients with PTB in whom both assays had been performed; the comparison is restricted to a single comparator in a single subgroup and requires prospective confirmation. Antibody levels were associated with radiographic extent under two of the three severity definitions examined, but not with cavitary disease; they are therefore regarded as investigational markers rather than established indicators of pulmonary TB or of radiographic severity.

research.abstract: PurposeTo evaluate whether fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO) combined with deep learning can detect metabolic signatures for classification of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). DesignCross-sectional analysis of participants included in the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with FLIO imaging. Subjects1,783 participants from the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with HbA1c measurements and FLIO imaging scans: 425 normoglycemic, 569 prediabetic, and 789 diabetic. MethodsGlycemic groups were defined from self-reported diagnosis, glucose-lowering medication, and HbA1c. Center-of-mass mean lifetime ({tau}CMM) maps, corrected for background and system timing offset, were generated from the raw time-resolved FLIO scans. Group differences in central-window {tau}CMM were tested by one-way ANOVA and by age-adjusted analysis of covariance. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), ResNet-18, and XGBoost were trained on {tau}CMM maps for three-class (normal, prediabetic, diabetic) and two binary (normal vs. impaired; normal vs. diabetic) classification of T2DM and compared them with an age-only classifier and with models combining FLIO and age. Main Outcome MeasuresMacro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, F1 score, and positive predictive value (PPV). ResultsGroup-averaged {tau}CMM was longer in prediabetic and diabetic than in normoglycemic participants in both the SSC (p < 0.001) and the LSC (p < 0.001), but only the SSC difference remained significant after age adjustment (p = 0.017). For 3-class classification, the CNN using FLIO achieved the highest AUROC (0.60 {+/-} 0.04), compared with 0.51 {+/-} 0.03 for an age-only classifier. ResNet-18 and XGBoost showed similar performance. Binary classification of normal vs. diabetic participants yielded AUROC 0.67 {+/-} 0.04 (CNN), 0.64 {+/-} 0.04 (ResNet-18), and 0.62 {+/-} 0.04 (XGBoost). All three FLIO models exceeded the age-only classifier in all T2DM classification tasks, whereas adding age to the FLIO models did not improve model performance. ConclusionsFLIO-derived {tau}CMM maps capture retinal signals associated with diabetes status that exceed what age alone provides, but yield modest classification performance with current artificial intelligence models. These findings highlight both the potential and the challenges of using FLIO for early metabolic screening and monitoring, informing future development of clinically applicable imaging biomarkers.

research.abstract: Tetrigidae is an early-branching family of Caelifera whose species live on damp ground, feed largely on mosses, algae and detritus, and often show wing and pronotum polymorphism. Which chemosensory and detoxification genes underlie this lifestyle is unknown. We generated an Oxford Nanopore PCR-cDNA transcriptome from a pooled sample of adult Hyboella guangxiensis (4.25 million full-length reads) and used it, together with protein homology, to filter the 17,996 machine-learning gene models of its chromosome-level genome to 15,338 supported genes without loss of BUSCO completeness. For nine families (OBP, CSP, IR, SNMP, P450, CCE, GST, UGT, ABC), full-length transcripts corrected 28 of 447 loci, including split and fused models, and brought protein lengths into agreement with orthologs of the sister species Bolivaritettix circocephalus (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.00066). Only 251 loci were supported by complete-ORF transcripts, and 101 had no full-length reads at all. Reconciliation of family phylogenies across eleven orthopteran genomes assigned 119 well-supported duplications to the Tetrigidae stem branch, dominated by P450 (42), UGT (27) and ABC (22) genes, and identified 63 homologous groups restricted to Tetrigidae. Five lineage-specific groups detected as transcripts in adults were validated at the genome level in four non-tetrigid outgroups: a CYP301A-like array, a Tetrigidae-specific UGT clade, two Tetrigidae-specific chemosensory proteins, a CYP9E2-like array and an esterase FE4-like array. Branch-site tests found episodic selection on some members of the UGT and CYP301A-like groups and in 7 of 28 recent paralog pairs, but not in the CYP9E2-like, FE4-like or CSP groups. These genes are candidates for the cuticular, chemosensory and dietary adaptations of pygmy grasshoppers to be tested with tissue-resolved data, whereas no family member could be linked to wing polymorphism.

research.abstract: Background/Objectives: Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the leading infectious causes of death worldwide, while multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB continue to pose major global health challenges. Kazakhstan is among the 30 high MDR-TB burden countries prioritized by the World Health Organization (WHO). This study aimed to assess national and regional trends in the burden of MDR-TB and XDR-TB in Kazakhstan between 2013 and 2022. Methods: We conducted a retrospective population-based study using anonymized case-level records of the National Tuberculosis Register of Kazakhstan for 2013-2022; duplicate registrations due to transfers were removed. Crude and age-standardized prevalence and mortality rates were calculated at the national and regional levels. Disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) were estimated as the sum of years of life lost (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD), following the Global Burden of Disease methodology, using WHO-based treatment durations and HIV-specific disability weights. The burden was additionally assessed by sex and age group, and associations between regional burden and socio-economic and health-system indicators were assessed using Spearman correlation and linear mixed models. Results: Between 2013 and 2022, crude MDR-TB prevalence decreased from 40.80 to 22.35 per 100,000 population (-45.2%) and XDR-TB prevalence from 2.12 to 0.05 per 100,000 (-97.8%). TB mortality among MDR-TB patients decreased by 71.5%, and no XDR-TB deaths were recorded in 2022. The age-standardized DALY rate of drug-resistant TB decreased from 97.0 to 27.8 per 100,000 (-71.3%). DALYs were 2.3-2.6 times higher among men than among women, with the greatest burden in working-age groups. In 2022, the highest burden was observed in West Kazakhstan, Kyzylorda and North Kazakhstan. DR-TB prevalence was higher in regions with more recipients of targeted social assistance, and per capita income was not associated with the burden; higher physician density was associated with lower DALY rates in the main analysis, but not consistently in sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: Kazakhstan experienced substantial reductions in the burden of MDR-TB and XDR-TB during 2013-2022. However, persistent sex and regional differences indicate that these improvements were not uniform across the population. Continued surveillance and targeted interventions in higher-burden population groups and regions remain important for further reducing the burden of drug-resistant TB.

research.abstract: Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTMs) are a large diverse group of opportunistic pathogens. The accurate identification of species within this genus is vital as pathogenicity, epidemiology, and treatment differ substantially between taxa. Whole-genome sequencing has improved taxonomic resolution, however current reference databases are likely incomplete. We analysed 53,170 high-quality mycobacterial genomes from 57,974 UK Health Security Agency samples collected between 2010 and 2025, a collection more than four times larger than the 12,726 mycobacterial genomes represented in GTDB release r232. High-quality isolates were assigned by average nucleotide identity (ANI) to recognised species within the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) using a 95% ANI threshold. Isolates that fell below this threshold were clustered using a minimal dominating set approach to identify genomically coherent groups consistent with being candidate novel species. Phylogenetic analysis of all Mycobacterium species was used to place the observed UK diversity in a global context and assess the ecological structure within the genus. Of the 850 Mycobacterial species-level reference genomes in GTDB, 204 GTDB references received at least one provisional assignment. We identified 586 (1.1%) high-quality isolates that could not be assigned to any GTDB species. Genomic clustering identified 110 additional candidate species-level references, expanding the reference set from 850 to 960 (12.9%). These candidate species were broadly distributed across the phylogeny. Within the Mycobacterium genus we found strong evidence that phylogenetic structure is associated with human (Fritz and Purvis D = 0.10, p<0.001) and environmental sources (D = 0.34, p<0.001). Together, existing and novel reference genomes resolved the UKHSA collection into 275 species-level clusters, of which 110 (40.0%) were not represented by existing GTDB references. Furthermore, source associations differed substantially between phylogenetic clades ({chi}{superscript 2} = 364 for human and {chi}{superscript 2} = 258 for environmental association; both p<0.001). Rarefaction analysis of the 275 species observed in UKHSA clinical samples did not plateau, with Chao1 estimation suggesting that additional sampling may reveal further novel species (Chao1 = 461). This study provides a comprehensive analysis of genomic NTM diversity within a large national surveillance collection. Our findings suggest that NTM diversity remains incompletely characterised, and supports the value of continued surveillance and curation to improve bacterial reference databases.

research.abstract: Understanding how crops adapt to environmental variation is crucial for biodiversity conservation and food security. Cucurbita pepo (pumpkin, squash, gourd), one of the earliest domesticated crops, exhibits remarkable phenotypic and ecological diversity, providing a valuable system for investigating the genomic basis of adaptation. Here, we constructed a graph-based C. pepo pangenome using nine chromosome-level assemblies and identified 229,431 high-confidence structural variants (SVs), which were genotyped across 206 wild and cultivated accessions. We reveal a history of parallel domestication, in which two deeply diverged gene pools independently gave rise to the cultivated pepo and ovifera lineages. Subsequent expansion into diverse environments was accompanied by pronounced genomic differentiation, with adaptive signatures largely associated with evolutionarily young alleles. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and SVs contribute complementary dimensions of environmental responsiveness. Biogeographical modeling predicts further range contractions of wild relatives and elevated genetic offset in Northern North American populations under projected future climates. Notably, populations with higher genetic load harbor fewer climate-associated variants and exhibit greater predicted genetic offset, revealing an association between deleterious mutation burden and reduced adaptive potential. These findings highlight how genomic variation, adaptive diversity, and genetic load together shape environmental adaptation and inform conservation and crop improvement.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Cultivated peanut ( Arachis hypogaea L.) is an allotetraploid crop (2n = 4x = 40) with an AABB genome that preserves extensive synteny between its two subgenomes. This characteristic, along with the availability of multiple genomic resources, provides a valuable framework for the comprehensive characterization of gene families and for inferring their evolutionary dynamics. Here we report a genome-wide analysis of the Dof transcription factor family in peanut (AhyDof), including phylogenetic inferences, gene structures, chromosomal locations, patterns of gene duplication, and expression analysis. Results ​A total of 66 non-redundant Dof genes (AhyDofs) were identified and unevenly distributed across the A and B subgenom​es. Comparative analyses revealed extensive conservation of gene structure, protein motifs, and chromosomal localization among homeologous genes inherited from the diploid progenitors, indicating that allopolyploidization contributed to family expansion while having a limited impact on gene diversification. Phylogenetic analyses placed AhyDofs within the four major angiosperm Dof lineages, supporting the evolutionary conservation of this family across flowering plants. Synteny analyses further identified chromosomal rearrangements and tandem duplication events contributing to the current composition of the AhyDof repertoire. Most notably, we discovered a novel group of six Dof genes associated with previously undescribed Pack-MULE transposons, designated AMuD, providing the first evidence of Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication in the genus Arachis . Structural and phylogenetic analyses suggested that these elements originated from non-autonomous MULEs and captured an ancestral Dof gene related to AhyDof-15.3. The dN/dS rate analysis suggested that transduplicated genes may have evolved under selective constraint, potentially indicating that functional constraints were maintained after mobilization. Comparative genomic analyses, PCR assays across diploid species, and Oxford Nanopore sequencing data suggested that AMuD elements originated within the B–F–K lineage of section Arachis and were maintained during peanut domestication and diversification. Promoter analyses revealed distinct cis-regulatory architectures among AMuD-derived genes, while transcriptomic data demonstrated their transcriptional activity, particularly in reproductive tissues. Conclusions The evolution of the peanut Dof repertoire in peanut was shaped by multiple mechanisms, including polyploidization, chromosomal rearrangements, tandem duplication, and lineage-specific Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication. The discovery of AMuD elements reveals a previously undescribed mechanism contributing to the diversification of regulatory genes in Arachis and provides new insights into the evolutionary dynamics of plant transcription factor families.

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Animal species differ dramatically in their overall size, yet the mechanisms underlying these differences are poorly understood. The Hippo pathway, first discovered in Drosophila , and widely conserved in mammals, regulates the nuclear levels of YAP1, a transcriptional co-activator that enhances the expression of growth-promoting genes. While experimental manipulations of this pathway elicit dramatic effects on tissue growth and organ size, it is not known whether, and to what extent, evolutionary divergence of this pathway has contributed to size differences across animals. Here we show that although YAP1 protein sequence is highly conserved between diverse mammals such as humans, elephants and blue whales, it diverges considerably among rodent species. While the human YAP1 protein is very similar to that of the largest rodent, the capybara Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris , those of smaller rodents such as the mouse Mus musculus and the vole Microtus oregoni show considerable divergence. An increased ratio of non-synonymous versus synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) in clades of small rodents compared to the background is indicative of relaxed constraint in these lineages, suggesting relative positive selection. When expressed in the developing Drosophila wing, capybara YAP1 was more potent at promoting growth than that of the mouse or vole. Following transfection into mammalian cells, capybara YAP1 is more effective at promoting expression of a reporter gene than either mouse or vole YAP1. Thus, by combining computational and experimental approaches, we show that evolutionarily divergent coding-region changes in YAP1 have likely contributed to the evolution of smaller body size in clades of rodents.

research.abstract: Abstract Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified the 10q26 locus as a major genetic risk factor for age-related macular degeneration (AMD), yet the causal variants and underlying mechanisms remain unresolved. Fine-mapping studies localized the AMD-associated region to a 5,196 bp interval near the ARMS2–HTRA1 locus, excluding both HTRA1 and the ARMS2 3′ indel variant as primary risk determinants. Using an unbiased bioinformatic approach based on protein–DNA interaction potential, we identified a polymorphic 5C/5A SNP streak within this interval predicted to alter binding of the non-receptor tyrosine kinase c-ABL. Electrophoretic mobility shift assays and chromatin immunoprecipitation–qPCR confirmed direct c-ABL binding to this regulatory element. The 5-SNP streak is in complete linkage disequilibrium with rs10490924 (A69S) and showed strong association with both wet AMD (OR = 3.37) and dry AMD (OR = 3.80) in 566 human DNA samples. Luciferase reporter assays demonstrated reduced transcriptional activity of the risk 5A haplotype in the presence of c-ABL. Consistent with these findings, ARMS2 mRNA expression was significantly increased (1.73-fold) in human RPE/choroid tissues carrying the risk 5A haplotype, whereas HTRA1 expression was unchanged. These results identify a functional noncoding regulatory element at 10q26 and implicate altered c-ABL–mediated regulation of ARMS2 in AMD pathogenesis.

research.abstract: BackgroundCulture-negative TB is a major diagnostic challenge, and the lack of a reliable reference standard hinders evaluation of non-sputum diagnostic tests. We compared composite reference criteria and Bayesian latent class analysis to examine how different culture-negative TB definitions affect disease classification and evaluations of two non-sputum biomarkers: urine lipoarabinomannan (uLAM) and host transcriptional response signatures (HRS). MethodsUrine and blood samples from 112 sputum culture-negative and 55 culture-positive symptomatic adults evaluated for tuberculosis from South Africa, Uganda, and Kenya, alongside 17 controls with other respiratory conditions, were analyzed using uLAM and HRS assays. Sensitivity and specificity were estimated for each assay based on three reference criteria: composite microbiological, composite clinical, and a latent class model. ResultsPositive classification proportions were 0.29 (32/112) and 0.46 (51/112) for the composite criteria and 0.20 (22/112) for the latent class model, with the Bayesian model estimating a prevalence of 0.31 (95%CrI 0.11-0.64). Sensitivity and specificity for uLAM ranged from 0.06-0.13 and 0.92-0.96, respectively. Sensitivity and specificity for HRS ranged from 0.47-0.78 and 0.56-0.69, respectively. uLAM results were significantly associated with microbiological positivity (OR=5.38, 95%CI=1.63-13.02). ConclusionThree distinct reference frameworks identified different individuals as having culture-negative TB while producing index assay sensitivity and specificity estimates with overlapping confidence and credible intervals, leading to similar conclusions regarding biomarker utility. This supports the use of complementary reference approaches to assess robustness to disease classification uncertainty in heterogeneous conditions such as culture-negative TB. SummaryWe evaluated potential sputum culture-negative TB using complementary diagnostic criteria and Bayesian latent class models, revealing extensive molecular and clinical diversity. Similar performance of two non-sputum diagnostic assays across reference frameworks supports triangulation when no single diagnostic gold standard exists.

research.abstract: Abstract Purpose The human 10q26 locus is a major genetic risk factor for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Fine mapping by linkage and large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has narrowed this region to a 30-kb interval encompassing the ARMS2 and HTRA1 genes. However, the causative gene(s), risk variants, and underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain unresolved. Methods Long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) candidates within the ARMS2–HTRA1 region were identified using human postmortem retinal RNA-seq data and public databases (NCBI, Ensembl). Candidate transcripts were validated by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing. Published single-cell RNA-seq datasets were analysed to define cell type–specific expression, and RNA levels were compared between AMD and non-AMD donor retinas. Additionally, expression changes were assessed in human iPSC-derived retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells exposed to cigarette smoke extract (CSE) and paraquat (PQT). Results We identified and characterized the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) HTRA1-AS1 and its transcript variants within the ARMS2 locus. HTRA1-AS1 overlaps ARMS2 and is transcribed in the antisense orientation. It is predominantly expressed in rod photoreceptors, Müller glia, and choroid/RPE tissues. Retinal HTRA1-AS1 expression was significantly reduced in AMD donors compared with controls (43 AMD vs. 44 controls, P = 0.007), whereas HTRA1 mRNA expression showed no significant difference (P = 0.121). In induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells, cigarette smoke extract (CSE)-induced oxidative stress markedly increased HTRA1-AS1 and ARMS2 expression by up to 8-fold and 75-fold, respectively, whereas paraquat treatment produced no significant changes. Conclusion These findings identify HTRA1-AS1 as an AMD-associated lncRNA within the ARMS2 locus that exhibits cell-type-specific expression, disease-associated downregulation, and responsiveness to cigarette smoke-induced oxidative stress. These results suggest that HTRA1-AS1 may contribute to AMD pathogenesis through noncoding regulatory mechanisms, warranting further functional investigation.

Here we identify a phenolic glycolipid (PGL) produced by the hypertransmissible Mtb strain HN878 as an additional activator of mouse and human nociceptive neurons, and we show that purified PGL is sufficient to induce cough in guinea pigs. Together, PGL and sulfolipid-1 elicit greater neuronal activation than either glycolipid alone. By synthesizing various PGL analogues, we show that neuroactivity depends on saccharide chain length and structure. Mechanistically, neurons release ATP extracellularly following PGL stimulation, which engages neuronal P2X3 purinergic receptors. This effect is blocked by a P2X3 antagonist, gefapixant. These findings reveal a neuronal activation pathway co-opted by certain Mtb strains to induce cough and suggest inhibition of purinergic signalling as a potential strategy to block airborne spread of Mtb.

research.abstract: Abstract Codon-based maximum likelihood models are the workhorse of molecular selection analysis, yet standard workflows assume that the input sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree are known without error. In practice, heuristic aligners ignore the genetic code and phylogeny, which packs non-homologous codons into shared columns across insertion-deletion loops and inflates gene-wide false-positive rates above 80%. This sequential division of labor is statistically suboptimal and computationally wasteful. Here, we present WALRUS ( W heatstone A lignment and L ikelihood R ate U nification for S election), a unified engine in H y P hy 3 ( https://github.com/veg/hyphy-3 ) that maps unaligned coding sequences to a coordinate-consistent selection atlas in one run. From a single Inside–Outside likelihood table, the pipeline repairs reading frames, co-estimates a codon alignment and Ohmic reticulate network, models directional base-composition drift, and evaluates eight selection tests (BUSTED-E, aBSREL, RELAX, FEL, dFEL, MEME, Contrast-FEL, and PRIME). Across 10,020 simulated alignments, WALRUS recovers 94.6% of true columns on the 800 INDELible replicates and cuts indel-driven false positives from 44.7%– 58.1% to 4.4% under BUSTED (21.1%– 21.4% to 1.4% under BUSTED-E). Under Zipfian indel saturation, false positives drop four-fold (33.3%– 83.3% to 17.0%– 20.5%), while 11, 190 avian orthogroup runs execute 6.6–35.8-fold faster and cut housekeeping false positives 13-fold (28-fold on ultraconserved genes) proteome-wide.

research.abstract: Background: The independent origins of plant parasitism in nematodes provide an ideal model for exploring the evolution of parasitic adaptations. Methods: Using a core set of 7 species and an expanded set of 16 species, we performed comparative genomic analyses across representative lineages of the suborder Tylenchina—specifically the superfamily Aphelenchoidea, family Anguinidae (superfamily Sphaerularioidea), and superfamily Tylenchoidea—to uncover the genetic basis of cross-superfamily molecular convergence and lineage-associated divergence. Results: Overall, sequence-level molecular convergence was relatively weak and may partly reflect the dilution of evolutionary signals by closely related ancestral backgrounds and the diverse genetic mechanisms driving the plant-parasitic phenotype. Nevertheless, independently evolved lineages exhibited recurrent functional themes in host interaction, barrier penetration, and nutrient acquisition. At the metabolic level, the unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis pathway (ko01040) showed consistent contraction across all phylogenetic models, pointing to a potential shift toward reliance on host-derived lipids. At the sequence level, a subset of genes displayed site-level convergence validated through independent alignment sets; these include homologs implicated in host recognition, effector folding, nitrogen metabolism, and stress perception at the host–pathogen interface. Pathway counts formed a continuous gradient rather than distinct groups, with 31 pathways demonstrating significant contraction (BH-FDR corrected PGLMM-NB2 model; median β = −0.31 and −0.77). Notably, 7 of the 12 convergent genes mapped to pathways undergoing contraction—including lipid/sphingolipid metabolism, oxidative phosphorylation, protein homeostasis, and nitrogen metabolism—indicating that sequence-level convergence and pathway-level reduction converge on shared functional modules. Conclusions: Together, these findings establish a comprehensive comparative genomic framework for understanding the origin and evolutionary radiation of plant parasitism in nematodes.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Whole-genome sequencing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) commonly relies on culture-derived isolates, potentially altering the bacterial populations represented. Direct sputum whole-genome sequencing (dsWGS) may better capture lineage composition and within-host variant diversity. Methods We compared targeted-enrichment dsWGS with WGS of matched culture-derived isolates from participants initiating treatment for rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in Worcester, South Africa. We assessed sequencing performance, technical reproducibility, sputum-sampling variability, lineage and variant concordance, and resistance-associated variation, and explored associations with baseline clinical characteristics and treatment response. Results Of 218 clinical dsWGS reactions, 139 passed sequencing quality criteria, yielding 113 eligible baseline sputum–culture pairs. Mixed-lineage infection was detected in 72/113 (63.7%) sputum specimens versus 7/113 (6.2%) matched cultures; 66/113 (58.4%) pairs showed reduced lineage diversity following culture. Permutation analysis indicated preferential retention of Lineage 2 and depletion of Lineage 3 after culture. Technical replicates preserved dominant phylotype assignments (median SNP Jaccard similarity 0.863), while independently collected sputum specimens showed greater variability. Among 38 concordant single-lineage pairs, 35,540/38,311 (92.8%) pair-specific variant observations were shared after filtering and raw-read recovery, while 2,497 (6.5%) were sputum-unique and 274 (0.7%) culture-unique. Discordance was concentrated among variable variants; 88.0% of shared variants variable in at least one specimen had higher allele frequencies in culture. No sputum-unique WHO Grade 1 or 2 resistance-associated mutations were identified in the strain-controlled subset, whereas eight mixed-lineage sputum samples versus three matched cultures harboured such mutations. Higher baseline low-frequency variant burden showed non-significant trends towards delayed culture conversion (log-rank p=0.144) and unfavourable treatment outcomes (log-rank p=0.400). Conclusions Direct-sputum WGS revealed M. tuberculosis lineage and low-frequency variant diversity that was not fully represented by matched culture-derived genomes, despite high overall genomic concordance. These findings highlight the complementary value of direct-sputum sequencing for characterising within-host diversity, while suggesting that the representation of bacterial populations following culture may vary across epidemiological settings. Further research is needed to improve the accuracy of minority-variant detection and establish the clinical relevance of diversity measured directly from sputum.

research.abstract: Abstract Orthology inference is foundational for comparative genomics, enabling the reconstruction of phylogenetic relationships and transfer of biological knowledge between species. Methods often infer different orthogroups and orthologous relationships, making robust benchmarking essential for evaluating their accuracy. Existing resources such as the Quest for Orthologs benchmark service and OrthoBench provide valuable benchmarks grounded in real biological data and expert curation. However, the true evolutionary histories in all of these benchmarks are unknown, and therefore the true accuracy of orthology inference methods is unknown. Simulations provide an approach to evaluate accuracy where the complete ground truth is known. However, simulations are only useful for benchmarking if they realistically reflect empirical data. Here, we introduce OrthoSimulator, a Python package for generating realistic, empirically calibrated benchmark datasets with known orthogroups, orthologous relationships, gene trees, and evolutionary events. We demonstrate its utility by benchmarking widely used orthology inference methods across simulations calibrated from multiple methods and empirical datasets. We show that method-to-method variability in ortholog inference accuracy is robust to variation in simulation parameters. We further provide a detailed evaluation of ortholog inference accuracy through independent cross-validation, and show that OrthoFinder is the most accurate of the four methods tested. OrthoSimulator is freely available at https://github.com/lauriebelch/OrthoSimulator . Significance Statement Comparative genomics relies on orthology, the identification of genes that descend from a single gene in a common ancestor. Many methods infer orthologs, and they often disagree, but their true accuracy is hard to measure because the true history of real genes is never known. We present OrthoSimulator, which learns from real genomes to simulate realistic gene families whose full history is recorded. The simulations complement existing benchmarks built from real genes by adding complete ground truth. We use them to compare four widely used methods and to measure errors that cannot be seen in real data, and the simulated genomes can test any method that reconstructs gene family evolution.

research.abstract: Abstract Taxonomic abundance data derived from 16S rRNA gene sequencing data are fundamental in microbiome research. To perform downstream statistical analysis and visualization, raw abundance data must typically be converted into standardized data structures, such as phyloseq S4 objects or BIOM files. This conversion requires three input data files: an Operational Taxonomic Unit (OTU) table (count of specific taxa across samples), a Taxonomy table (hierarchical lineage from Kingdom to Species), and a Sample Data table (experimental metadata). For Oxford Nanopore (ONT) 16S data, the two commonly used classifiers, Emu and the EPI2ME wf-16s workflow (Minimap2/Kraken2), generate output files with different formats and column schemas. We found no web-based tool that accepts these classifier outputs directly. Experienced users can reshape them with a script. Researchers who do not program cannot, and for them, this step remains a hurdle. We introduce VPHYL(Versatile PHYLogenetic Standardizer), an R Shiny web application that accepts abundance outputs directly from Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s, splits the lineage into standard ranks, attaches sample metadata, and generates phyloseq objects or BIOM files. VPHYL integrates multi-file aggregation and produces automated HTML reports comprising read statistics, alpha diversity metrics, and taxonomic abundance visualizations. VPHYL output was identical to that of an independently written R script for all nine supported classifier-database combinations. We validated the framework by processing raw abundance datasets processed using the EPI2ME Labs 16S Workflow from a published respiratory microbiome study comprising both porcine and human microbiota composition samples. The published tables were processed by VPHYL without modification, and the resulting alpha diversity indices and taxonomic profiles were consistent with the reported findings; small differences reflect read filtering applied in the original study. The application is publicly available at https://venkat-247.shinyapps.io/VPHYL/ .

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Synonymous codon usage bias (CUB) provides a complementary perspective on molecular variation, but its relationship with morphological diversity in rapidly radiating plant lineages remains poorly understood. We investigated this relationship in Thelypteridaceae by integrating chloroplast phylogenomics, codon usage analyses, and published descriptions of lamina base architecture. A phylogeny based on 31 shared protein‐coding genes provided the evolutionary framework for 37 plastome accessions, including two outgroups. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) revealed three major codon usage groupings (Types A–C) that partly differed from the chloroplast phylogeny, with Types A and C corresponding descriptively to contrasting lamina base forms. A focused comparison of 27 accessions and eight genes retained this Type A–Type C separation. Although ENC, PR2, and neutrality plots showed broadly similar overall patterns between the types, gene‐wise analyses highlighted ndhJ, psaA, and psbD, and protein‐guided codon alignments reproduced their type‐specific synonymous third‐position counts. These complementary observations support a relationship between chloroplast codon usage variation and frond architecture in the sampled taxa. They identify candidate photosynthesis‐related loci and provide a basis for testing the evolutionary and functional processes underlying this relationship.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis remains a major health burden around the world. With the emergence of multi-drug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the need for alternative antimicrobial strategies has increased. Bacteriophages can specifically infect and lyse bacteria, thereby having the potential for the treatment of tuberculosis. Administration via pulmonary delivery may offer a means of concentrating viable bacteriophages at the infection site within the deep lung while reducing systemic exposure. This review examines the pathophysiological and intracellular barriers relevant to pulmonary TB and evaluates current strategies for aerosolized phage delivery, including nebulization, dry-powder formulations, and macrophage-targeted delivery systems. Preclinical studies demonstrate promising aerosol performance, intracellular delivery, and antimycobacterial activity, particularly through engineered dry powders and liposomal systems; however, direct clinical evidence in pulmonary TB remains limited. Major challenges include maintaining phage viability during aerosol generation and storage, penetrating granulomatous lesions, and delivering sufficient active phages to intracellular M. tuberculosis within alveolar macrophages. Future translation will depend on improving phage stability during aerosolization, achieving efficient alveolar and intracellular delivery, overcoming host and lesion barriers, and establishing standardized manufacturing, safety, and regulatory frameworks.

research.abstract: Abstract Cytochrome P450 (CYP) genes form a large and functionally diverse superfamily of heme-thiolate monooxygenases that catalyse the oxidation of endogenous and exogenous compounds. Within this superfamily, CYP4 enzymes primarily act on fatty acids, substrates central to energy metabolism. Sustained flight and long distance migration in birds rely on efficient fatty acid use, making CYP4 a pertinent system for examining how lipid associated functions may vary across avian lineages. Here, we characterised the evolution of CYP4 genes across 363 avian whole genomes, representing over 90% of bird families, to investigate patterns of molecular evolution and their association with ecological and life history variation. We identified four CYP4 subfamilies and analysed sequence evolution using site-models, branch-models, and branch-site models. Our analyses revealed conserved elements of the avian CYP4 repertoire alongside lineage-specific heterogeneity in selective constraint. Several amino acid sites under positive selection were located within substrate recognition sites, regions influencing substrate binding and catalysis. Branch-model analyses identified trait-associated variation in selective pressure across feeding habits, migration and primary lifestyle, with gene-specific patterns. Migration-associated differences in ω remained below one, indicating variation in the strength of selective constraint among migration categories. Branch-site analyses revealed evidence of episodic positive selection associated with migratory lineages. Overall, these results highlight site-specific adaptive evolution within CYP4 genes alongside broader variation in selective constraint, providing insight into the evolution of lipid associated metabolic pathways during avian diversification.

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Hepatic tuberculosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation that may mimic hepatobiliary malignancy or complex cystic lesions, resulting in diagnostic challenges. Case Presentation: A 36-year-old Filipino woman without recognized immunocompromising conditions presented with fever, weight loss, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Imaging showed a multiloculated cystic lesion in hepatic segments V/VI with focal biliary prominence. Liver biopsy demonstrated necrotizing and non-necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with focally positive Ziehl-Neelsen staining. Tissue MTB-PCR detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis without rifampicin resistance, and culture confirmed M. tuberculosis complex susceptible to streptomycin, isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol. CT chest showed diffuse bilateral micronodules in a miliary pattern; initial sputum smear and PCR were negative, but final sputum culture became positive at 6 weeks. Standard 2HRZE/4HR therapy was initiated, with clinical and biochemical improvement at 1 month. Conclusion: Hepatic tuberculosis should be considered in atypical cystic hepatic lesions, and tissue diagnosis is essential to avoid unnecessary invasive procedures.

research.abstract: Introduction Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) Lineage 2 (East Asian, Beijing) strains are globally distributed and frequently associated with multidrug resistance, yet their genomic diversity in Ecuador remains uncharacterized. Methdos We performed a whole-genome comparative analysis of all the seven available MTB Beijing strains isolated in Ecuador—two newly sequenced in this study and five retrieved from public repositories—contextualized against 53 regional (Peru, Colombia, Brazil) and globally representative reference genomes. Lineage assignment and resistance genotyping used TB-Profiler; core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms (cgSNPs) were called with Snippy against H37Rv after masking 612,282 bp of repetitive, mobile, and drug-resistance-associated regions, and a maximum-likelihood phylogeny was inferred from 3,473 variable sites across 59 taxa with IQ-TREE. Results Six isolates were assigned to the modern sublineage 2.2.1 and one to the ancestral sublineage 2.2.2. Two isolates returned a mixed Lineage 2/Lineage 4 signal and were excluded as chimeric assemblies. The five remaining genomes did not form a single clade: four modern isolates clustered together with maximal support, whereas the ancestral isolate branched among Asian ancestral lineages, differed from the other Ecuadorian isolates by 511–530 SNPs, and was most closely related to a Turkmen genome (129 SNPs). This topology would suggest at least two independent introductions of the Beijing lineage into Ecuador. Modern isolates lay closer to South American genomes (100–126 SNPs) than to any global reference (≥167 SNPs) but showed no country-specific affinity, and all fell well outside the Peruvian pre-extensively drug-resistant transmission cluster (1–32 SNPs internally). Resistance profiles included three genotypically predicted susceptible isolates, three multidrug-resistant isolates, and one pre-extensively drug-resistant isolate. Two distinct rpoB alleles (p.His445Tyr and p.Asp435Val) mapped to phylogenetically distant positions among the five clonal isolates, consistent with independent acquisition of rifampicin resistance; a third allele (p.Ser450Leu), identified in the excluded mixed-lineage isolates, was attributed to their dominant Lineage 4 component. Conclusion These findings provide a first insight into phylogenomic characterization of the MTB Beijing lineage in Ecuador and underscore the need for expanded, population-based genomic surveillance of tuberculosis in the Andean region.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Riboflavin biosynthesis is required for in vitro survival of the human pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ). However, despite the lack of a known transporter, growth can be rescued by exogenous riboflavin. The riboflavin biosynthesis pathway is also predicted essential in vivo , but whether riboflavin levels available in the host can support survival has not been directly tested. Here we constructed a set of inducible CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) knockdown and targeted gene deletion strains for known riboflavin biosynthesis genes ( ribA2, ribG, ribH, ribC ) as tools to characterize riboflavin requirements, uptake, and metabolite changes and to assess in vivo essentiality. We found that riboflavin, but not flavin adenine dinucleotide or flavin mononucleotide, rescued auxotrophy for all strains tested. Further, riboflavin uptake was not affected by disruption of proton motive force or ATP synthesis, suggesting that uptake is not via an active mechanism. Targeted metabolite profiling after removal of riboflavin from growth medium confirmed reduced riboflavin levels. While other riboflavin intermediates were not detected, significant accumulation of aromatic amino acids (Phe, Tyr) was observed across all assayed strains, as well as alteration in a vitamin B9 metabolite. Selecting the ribC knockout as a representative strain, we found that riboflavin depletion had a bacteriostatic effect as late as 3 weeks after removal. Unexpectedly, Δ ribC lacked infectivity in an aerosol mouse infection, suggesting that the potential to scavenge riboflavin from the host is not sufficient to survive in vivo . Overall, our results show that altered metabolism upon loss of riboflavin biosynthesis leads to compromised Mtb infectivity. IMPORTANCE Tuberculosis remains one of the world’s most deadly infectious diseases, underscoring the need to explore new drug targets. Riboflavin (vitamin B2) biosynthesis has emerged as a promising target because Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) depends on this pathway for survival. The riboflavin pathway also produces metabolites that modulate host mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cell activity, towards understanding potential strategies for host-directed therapies. Here we found that disrupting riboflavin biosynthesis led to not only compromised survival, but also widespread changes to metabolism and loss of the ability to establish infection in an animal model. These findings improve our understanding of how Mtb adapts to metabolic stress, with implications for developing drugs that target riboflavin biosynthesis and for alterations in host immunity to be explored in future studies.

research.abstract: Abstract Motivation Pathogen phylogenies are useful for monitoring the evolution of pathogens and for detecting new variants, as it provides information that can aid public health decisions and outbreak response. Since not all infections are sequenced, certain pathogen lineages may be missing or only poorly represented in reconstructed phylogenies. Identifying these gaps could help to determine where additional data collection is required. Results We developed a computational method to locate regions of missing samples from the observed tree alone, without sequences from those samples. A machine learning model predicts which branches lead toward the missing region. Beam search then identifies three representative paths and estimates a candidate most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of the missing region for each path. We tested this framework on 5,000 simulated phylogenies where we controlled which tips were deleted. On an independent test set, the best candidate recovered an average of 89.9% of deleted tips, increasing to 90.7% when all three candidates were combined. Predicted and true MRCAs lay on the same ancestral–descendant lineage in 91.3% of cases. We further evaluated the approach on an empirical SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny with introduced missingness. By identifying potentially underrepresented lineages, this framework could help real-time identification of missing infections and improve outbreak response. research.abstract: Congenital tuberculosis is an uncommon but clinically severe manifestation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection that remains challenging to diagnose because of its nonspecific neonatal presentation and delayed maternal diagnosis. This narrative review examines current evidence on epidemiology, clinical presentation, treatment and prevention, with particular emphasis on maternal disease, the maternal-fetal interface, and mechanisms underlying vertical transmission; as an original component, we also performed a case-level curation of published maternal and congenital tuberculosis reports to characterize their geographic distribution. Fetal exposure is more likely in active maternal tuberculosis, particularly when disease is disseminated, extrapulmonary, or genital, with additional risk associated with delayed diagnosis, inadequate treatment, drug resistance, and comorbidities. Vertical transmission may occur through transplacental hematogenous dissemination, aspiration or ingestion of infected amniotic fluid, or exposure to infected genital secretions during delivery. Experimental evidence supports the biological plausibility of placental infection and persistence, although direct mechanistic evidence remains limited. Diagnosis requires integration of maternal history, neonatal findings, microbiological or molecular testing, imaging, and placental examination when available. Early maternal diagnosis and appropriate treatment remain the most effective preventive strategies. Future research should prioritize multicenter prospective cohorts, standardized maternal-neonatal follow-up, and physiologically relevant human models to clarify transmission mechanisms and identify biomarkers of risk.

Methods We analyzed European-ancestry genome-wide association study (GWAS) data for ADHD (38,691 cases; 186,843 controls) and BPD (12,339 cases; 1,041,717 controls). Linkage disequilibrium score regression, conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR), bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR), MR accounting for linkage disequilibrium and sample overlap (MR-LAP), Causal Analysis Using Summary Effect estimates (CAUSE), colocalization, and Sum of Single Effects (SuSiE) fine-mapping assessed genetic sharing and directionality. Results Genetic correlation was substantial (r_g = 0.733). ConjFDR identified 48 shared loci; 36 (75%) showed concordant directions in both phenotype-specific comparisons. Functional annotation implicated axon guidance, oxidative phosphorylation, and developing midbrain cells. ADHD-to-BPD MR was positive (22 instruments; inverse-variance weighted beta = 0.487, SE = 0.082, p = 3.27 × 10^-9), persisting after outlier removal, MR-LAP correction, and exclusion of two instruments at colocalized loci. Reverse MR was positive (five instruments; beta = 0.303, SE = 0.112, p = 6.83 × 10^-3) but heterogeneous and variant-sensitive. CAUSE favored directional over sharing-only models in both directions (delta ELPD = 6.98 and 5.92, respectively). SuSiE colocalization supported shared signals at rs17576773, rs9969232, and rs4727799. Conclusions ADHD and BPD exhibit extensive genetic overlap involving 48 shared loci and convergent evidence of directional associations. Findings across complementary methods more consistently support an ADHD-to-BPD relationship, suggesting that shared genetic susceptibility alone may not fully explain their co-occurrence.

research.abstract: Abstract Enterobacter species are opportunistic pathogens whose identification is complicated by closely related lineages and changing species nomenclature. We reassessed 1,074 public genomes using average nucleotide identity (ANI), type-strain comparisons and phylogenies based on conserved markers, genome alignments and k-mers. Among 1,070 genomes included in the classification comparison, 123 changed species or subspecies membership relative to NCBI labels, 499 changed names following revisions to species boundaries or ranks, and 69 previously unnamed genomes received species assignments. The oharae, steigerwaltii, xiangfangensis and hoffmannii lineages formed an expanded Enterobacter xiangfangensis , separate from the lineage containing the E. hormaechei type. We propose five transferred combinations: E. xiangfangensis subsp. oharae comb. nov., E. xiangfangensis subsp. steigerwaltii comb. nov., E. xiangfangensis subsp. hoffmannii comb. nov., E. roggenkampii subsp. quasiroggenkampii comb. nov. and E. chengduensis subsp. rongchengensis comb. nov. We also describe the corresponding type subspecies, E. xiangfangensis subsp. xiangfangensis comb. nov., E. roggenkampii subsp. roggenkampii comb. nov. and E. chengduensis subsp. chengduensis comb. nov., and emend the descriptions of E. xiangfangensis and E. hormaechei . E. dykesii and E. quasimori are treated as later heterotypic synonyms of E. asburiae and E. mori , respectively. Within E. xiangfangensis subsp. hoffmannii , we define 25 genomic groups (genomovars) at 99.5% ANI. Conflicting tree relationships leave the position of E. ludwigii and the branching order of the hoffmannii-associated types unresolved. We developed Pterobacter to apply the revised classifications to assemblies, using alignment-based ANI near the species boundary and withholding assignments when the reference evidence is insufficient.

research.abstract: Background Aging-related genes (ARGs) may contribute to immune heterogeneity in tuberculosis (TB), but their diagnostic and biological relevance remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify TB-associated ARG transcripts, characterize their immune and molecular correlates, and evaluate their exploratory diagnostic performance across prespecified cohorts. Patients and methods Public TB transcriptomic cohorts were analyzed together with a local bulk RNA-seq cohort comprising 5 TB patients and 5 controls and a local single-cell RNA-seq cohort comprising 3 active TB patients and 3 controls. The local cohorts were selected using random sampling. Age-adjusted differential expression, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, machine-learning-based feature selection, immune-infiltration analysis, consensus clustering, single-cell annotation, and Comparative Toxicogenomics Database-based compound-gene screening were performed. Results GSE83456 included 45 TB patients and 61 controls. Age-adjusted differential expression identified 189 differentially expressed genes, and the intersection of DEGs, ARGs, and blue-module genes yielded 11 discovery candidates. Nested model selection in GSE83456 identified a naive Bayes classifier based on STAT1, PLAUR, JAK2, and P2RY14. Across five repeated stratified nested cross-validation runs, the mean AUC was 0.962, with a repeat-level range of 0.954-0.969. Balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 0.926, 0.911, 0.941, and 0.928, respectively. Exploratory evaluations included GSE19439, GSE34608, GSE62525, GSE19444, and the local RNA-seq cohort. Consensus clustering separated TB samples into two ARG-associated subgroups with distinct immune-infiltration and pathway-activity profiles. CIBERSORT analysis identified significant TB-control differences in 9 of 22 inferred immune-cell types. Single-cell analysis demonstrated heterogeneous expression of STAT1, PLAUR, JAK2, and P2RY14 across annotated immune-cell subsets. CTD screening generated exploratory compound-gene associations that provide testable hypotheses for future experimental studies. Conclusion Age-adjusted multi-cohort analysis identified candidate ARG-associated TB markers and immune patterns. STAT1, PLAUR, JAK2, and P2RY14 are candidate markers rather than clinically validated biomarkers and require independent experimental and clinical validation.

research.abstract: Abstract Genome assemblies are accumulating rapidly across the Tree of Life, creating a growing need for reproducible and scalable methods for whole-genome comparison. We developed nf-core/pairgenomealign, a Nextflow workflow that automates pairwise genome alignment using the LAST software suite and produces standard alignment, visualisation, and summary outputs. The pipeline supports a wide range of evolutionary distances, runs reproducibly across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments, and exports alignments in formats including MAF, BAM, BCF, and CRAM. We repurposed the compact format used for sequencing reads to combine the alignments of many genomes to the same target into a single file, which genome browsers display directly and from which multiple sequence alignments of any region can be extracted. Benchmarking against established genome aligners shows competitive performance with tunable trade-offs between speed and sensitivity, while applications to comparative genomics and assembly quality control illustrate its uses.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB) is able to survive and replicate within host cells of the myeloid cell lineage, a critical step in the development of active TB, achieved through multiple immune evasion mechanisms. TRPML1 (Mucolipin 1), a non-selective Ca 2+ ion channel belonging to the TRP superfamily, is predominantly expressed in innate immune cells and is localized intracellularly along the endosomal-lysosomal continuum. TRPML1-mediated Ca 2+ signalling is vital for lysosomal biogenesis and trafficking processes essential for effective immune responses. The mechanisms regulating TRPML1 channel function in myeloid cells during mycobacterial infection remain poorly characterized. METHODS: During in vitro infection, TRPML1 expression was modulated in a time-dependent manner by Mtb and M. bovis BCG in murine macrophages, as well as in human neutrophils (PMNs) and macrophages (MDMs). Using pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 channel activity, we observed alterations in intracellular Ca 2+ concentrations following Mtb infection. RESULTS: Here, we describe distinct TRPML1 expression patterns in granulomas from TB patients who had completed treatment for active TB, suggesting a potential role for TRPML1 in pathogenesis. We further demonstrate that Mtb infection is associated with altered TRPML1 expression and intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis, accompanied by changes in ROS production, necrotic cell death and enhanced mycobacterial survival within host cells. Treatment of PMN-MDM cocultures with a TRPML1 antagonist, but not an agonist, was associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and necrotic cell death. DISCUSSION: Here, we show that Mtb-mediated disruption of TRPML1 function is associated with altered intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis and may contribute to impaired phagosome maturation, a process previously linked to TRPML1-dependent endolysosomal function, thereby potentially favoring mycobacterial survival within host cells. These findings suggest that Mtb-induced alterations in TRPML1 associated cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis may impair Ca²⁺-dependent ROS production and cell death, potentially affecting intracellular Mtb survival. Our findings support a role for TRPML1 in maintaining myeloid cell Ca²⁺ homeostasis and suggest that TRPML1 may contribute to the innate immune response to Mtb infection.

research.abstract: Abstract Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (CRKP) is among the most urgent antimicrobial-resistance threats, yet its extraordinary capsular diversity has kept phage therapy locked in per-isolate matching — a process too slow and labor-intensive for routine use. Here we convert this specificity problem into a look-up problem. Interrogating 26,138 CRKP genomes from 96 countries, we show that capsular diversity collapses onto a tractable target list: 14 capsular locus (KL) types dominate contemporary circulation and jointly account for 67–77% of the CRKP burden in every WHO region, stably from 2010 to 2024 and after removal of sampling bias. We assembled a repository of 48 strictly lytic phages spanning all 14 types and organized it into capsule-defined modules: for eight KL types a single capsule-targeting phage sufficed to prevent resistant regrowth over 24 h, and for the remaining six a two-phage module pairs a capsule-targeting phage with a capsule-independent phage that recognizes the second receptor layer exposed upon capsule loss. We treated 28 clinical isolates, covering two distinct STs for each of the 14 KL types. Modules were assigned from the KL call alone, without isolate-level matching data. Growth was suppressed in every strain, and ST background had no significant effect in 12 of 14 types. These results establish capsule type, not lineage, as the operative unit of CRKP phage preparedness: a single rapid KL-typing step converts a diagnostic result into a therapeutic decision, providing a practical, lineage-agnostic route from surveillance to treatment.

research.abstract: Abstract Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive. research.abstract: BACKGROUND: The prevalence and evolution of drug resistance in TB pose a persistent threat to global TB control. Understanding the epidemiological characteristics, population distribution, and temporal trends of drug resistance is crucial for evaluating the effectiveness of prevention and control measures and adjusting strategies accordingly. METHODS: This study retrospectively analyzed 9,665 clinical isolates of Mycobacterium TB collected between 2015 and 2024. Drug susceptibility testing was performed using the proportion method to detect resistance to isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, streptomycin, and levofloxacin. The chi-square test was used to compare differences between groups, and the chi-square test for trend was applied to analyze temporal changes in drug resistance. RESULTS: The overall drug resistance rate was 20.87% (2017/9665, 95% CI: 20.06%-21.69%), and the MDR rate was 10.25% (991/9665, 95% CI: 9.66%-10.88%). Drug resistance rates varied significantly among different populations, with males (1528/6730,22.70%; 95% CI: 21.71%-23.72%) exhibiting higher rates than females (489/2935,16.66%; 95% CI: 15.33%-18.06%), and the 19-59 age group (1511/6788,22.26%; 95% CI: 21.27%-23.27%) showing higher rates than the ≤ 18 (124/694,17.87%; 95% CI: 15.09%-20.92%) and ≥ 60 age groups (382/2183, 17.50%; 95% CI: 15.93%-19.16%). Over the ten-year period, the overall drug resistance rate showed a significant upward trend (from 17.29% to 22.98%). Rates of single drug resistance, PDR, and resistance to streptomycin and levofloxacin also increased significantly. In contrast, the MDR rate and resistance rates to rifampicin and ethambutol did not show significant trends. CONCLUSION: The TB drug resistance problem in this region is severe, with a rapid increase in resistance to the key second-line drug levofloxacin, indicating significant challenges for the current prevention and control system. Targeted interventions for populations with higher resistance rates, such as males and young adults, along with strengthened antibiotic stewardship, are critical to curbing the further spread of drug resistance.

However, recent genome-based studies have created taxonomic ambiguity by either assigning related strains directly to the taxon Ca. P. pruni or separating them into more than one genomic cluster without formal taxonomic classification or proposing new taxon for new divergent strains. In this study, we sequenced genomes of the pecan bunchy top phytoplasma (PBT), previously designated a “ Ca. P. pruni-related strain,” initially to confirm the pathogen in an Oklahoma pecan orchard. Phylogenomic comparisons with previously sequenced Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni strains revealed four well-supported taxonomic groups based on average nucleotide identity, digital DNA–DNA hybridization, and phylogenetic analyses, with different host ecologies consistent with International Research Programme on Comparative Mycoplasmology (IRPCM) guidelines for assigning new taxon. Accordingly, we propose a reclassification of Ca. P. pruni and related strains into four species: Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni, representing the taxon associated with X-disease phytoplasma; three proposed new Candidatus species including Candidatus Phytoplasma caryae sp. nov, Candidatus Phytoplasma conii sp. nov and Candidatus Phytoplasma lactucae sp. nov. The study provides comparative-genomic insights into these taxonomic groups that support their evolution.

research.abstract: Background/Objectives: Treatment for drug-resistant tuberculosis involves a long duration and a heavy burden of drug-induced hepatotoxicity; drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is a significant issue affecting treatment safety. The Dietary Inflammation Index (DII) quantifies the pro-inflammatory potential of the diet, but evidence linking it to the risk of DILI in patients with drug-resistant tuberculosis is limited. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between DII and the risk of treatment-related liver injury in patients with drug-resistant tuberculosis. Methods: A prospective cohort of patients with drug-resistant tuberculosis was established at Hunan Provincial Chest Hospital, with a 6-month follow-up period during which liver function was assessed monthly. DILI was identified based on liver function abnormalities and causality was assessed using the Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM), with a RUCAM score > 3 considered indicative of DILI. The Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) was calculated using a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire, and participants were classified into anti-inflammatory, neutral, and pro-inflammatory groups using K-means clustering. Logistic regression was used to evaluate the association between DII and DILI after adjustment for potential confounders, including age, sex, BMI, smoking, alcohol consumption, and medication use. L1 regularization, restricted cubic spline analysis, and subgroup analyses were further performed to assess the robustness and potential nonlinear patterns of the association. Results: A total of 800 participants were enrolled; 729 completed follow-up, and 69 developed DILI, resulting in a cumulative incidence of 9.4%. The risk of DILI was significantly higher in the pro-inflammatory group than in the anti-inflammatory group: OR = 2.17 (95% CI: 1.17-4.05) in Model 1, and OR = 2.19 (95% CI: 1.16-4.14) after adjustment; For every 1-unit increase in DII, the risk of liver injury increased by approximately 29% (OR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.08-1.54). Results from L1 regularization were consistent, and effect modification was observed at the levels of sex and age. Conclusions: A higher Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) was an independent risk factor for antituberculosis treatment-related liver injury in patients with drug-resistant tuberculosis. The risk of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) in the pro-inflammatory dietary group was approximately twice that in the anti-inflammatory dietary group. Identifying and modifying pro-inflammatory dietary patterns may help reduce the risk of DILI and improve the safety of antituberculosis treatment.

research.abstract: Aythya, comprising 12 species, is a group of ducks that forage by diving. Diving foraging is a high-energy-consuming activity, as aquatic environments can lead to substantial energy loss. Therefore, Aythya species require efficient energy production to maintain body temperature and meet high energy demands. Mitochondria are important energy-producing organelles that harbor their own genomes. Thus, the mitochondrial genome DNA (mtDNA) of Aythya species might be subject to different selective constraints compared with that of Anas species, which seldom exhibit diving foraging behavior. However, the characterization and evolution patterns of mtDNA in Aythya and their differences from Anas remain unclear. Therefore, we assembled three mitochondrial genomes from Aythya species (Aythya affinis, Aythya collaris, and Aythya innotata) and four from Anas species (Anas bahamensis, Anas capensis, Anas flavirostris, and Anas georgica) based on genome data from the publicly available Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database. These mitochondrial genomes exhibit the canonical genomic features of avian mitochondrial genomes in the family Anatidae. We then compared the evolutionary rates of the mitochondrial protein-coding genes (PCGs) of nine Aythya species with those of twelve Anas species. The free-ratios model results indicated that the 13 PCGs were mainly under purifying selection in both Aythya and Anas species, with purifying selection being slightly stronger in Aythya than that in Anas species. In addition, ND5 was detected as a rapidly evolving gene (REG) in the Aythya clade through the two- and one-ratio models. In summary, this study provides insights into the composition and evolutionary patterns of mitochondrial genomes in Aythya and offers new mitochondrial genome resources for future research.

research.abstract: Abstract The cellular composition and spatial organization of immune responses within tuberculosis (TB) granulomas have been increasingly characterized, yet how these spatially organized immune cell populations coordinate local adaptive immunity remains largely unknown. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and immune receptor profiling to construct a comprehensive spatial atlas of human TB granulomas. We identified two concentric adaptive immune niches surrounding the central necrotic core. The outer niche comprised granuloma-associated tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) that supported T FH -B cell interactions and exhibited functional germinal center-like features associated with antigen-driven B-cell maturation toward FCRL5⁺ antibody-producing cells. The inner niche contained antigen-experienced and Mtb -reactive effector memory CD8⁺ T cells (T EM ), which were recruited from distal lung regions by LGALS9 high chemokine-expressing macrophages and activated to undergo local clonal expansion. In lgals9l1 deficient zebrafish, macrophage depletion was accompanied by marked reductions in T– and B-cell enrichment within granulomas and increased bacterial loads, supporting a role for LGALS9 high macrophages in coordinating local adaptive immunity against TB infection. Finally, AI-based prediction of spatial gene expression from clinical hematoxylin and eosin-stained specimens revealed that inferred TLS abundance increased with TB disease severity. These findings identify spatially interconnected adaptive immune niches that organize protective immune responses within human TB granulomas, therefore providing a foundation for understanding granuloma adaptive immunity and developing host-directed therapies and vaccines for TB ( https://tbomics.smart-nbc.org.cn/ ).

research.abstract: Empyema necessitans is a rare complication of pleural infection in which infected pleural fluid extends through the parietal pleura into the surrounding soft tissues. We report the case of a 32-year-old man of Indian origin living in the United Kingdom who presented with worsening right-sided pleuritic chest pain, several months of night sweats, and a persistent dry cough. Five months earlier, he had been treated for right-sided pneumonia complicated by a pleural effusion, with persistent radiographic abnormalities on follow-up. Examination revealed reduced right-sided air entry and a tender, fluctuant swelling over the right posterior chest wall. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a posterior pleural collection extending through the chest wall into the adjacent paraspinal musculature, consistent with empyema necessitans. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded frank purulent fluid. Routine bacterial, anaerobic, and fungal cultures were negative. Acid-fast bacilli were not seen on initial microscopy; however, mycobacterial culture became positive after seven days, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the pleural fluid detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Whole-genome sequencing subsequently identified a lineage 1 East-African-Indian-Ocean isolate with predicted susceptibility to first-line antituberculous agents. Four-drug antituberculous therapy was commenced, with subsequent clinical and radiological improvement. This case highlights chest wall swelling as an unusual presentation of tuberculosis and emphasizes the importance of cross-sectional imaging and targeted mycobacterial testing in establishing the diagnosis.

Here, we assembled and annotated the complete linear mitogenome of P. zanlanscianense and analysed its gene repertoire, codon usage, repeats, RNA editing sites, MTPTs, synteny, phylogeny and Ka/Ks. research.abstract: Agrobacteria transfer T-DNA (transferred DNA) into plant genomes, and remnants persist in many plants. Whether fungi carry such genes has not been examined systematically. We searched 6123 fungal proteomes and 2215 genome assemblies for homologs of eleven T-DNA opine synthesis genes. Most homologs belong to native fungal families, from which we separated acquired genes by reverse searches, phylogenies and contamination tests. Seven groups of genes are of rhizobial origin; where the flanking DNA could be examined, they are embedded in fungal chromosomes, not carried on contaminating bacterial DNA. Three groups are closest to the T-DNA genes sus, cus and chs; four are related to other rhizobial genes of opine metabolism, including a three-gene opine dehydrogenase island of Fusarium matching an Agrobacterium larrymoorei plasmid locus. Five groups are concentrated in the ectomycorrhizal family Boletaceae, where they co-occur in mosaic islands combining genes from several plasmid loci; cus-like genes of other fungi fall into at least five separate clades, consistent with repeated acquisitions. The sus-, cus- and chs-like genes show evidence of purifying selection, genes in the Fusarium island are transcribed, and other groups decay. These findings show contrasting fates of acquired genes in fungi.
